title: Mahalia Jackson
hook: the queen of gospel, who sang at the great civil rights march in the capital

segments.voice: Yesterday, a packed hall in Dublin and a chorus that won't stop saying it. Your line was and he shall reign. Did you hum it when the news got loud? Day nine hundred ninety-three.

A crowd stretches down the National Mall in the capital, all the way along the reflecting pool. It's hot. There have been speeches all afternoon. Then a woman steps up to the microphones at the Lincoln Memorial, and she doesn't give a speech. She sings. An old spiritual about being scorned and put down, sung slow and huge, and the crowd goes still. A little later, Martin Luther King Jr. is speaking, and the story is told that she called out to him from behind: tell them about the dream, Martin. However it happened, he moved away from his prepared text. Her name was Mahalia Jackson. Today, the woman people called the queen of gospel.

Mahalia Jackson grew up in New Orleans and sang in church from childhood. She moved north to Chicago and kept singing, in storefront churches, at funerals, anywhere they'd have her. Gospel music in that city was being shaped by people like Thomas A. Dorsey, a songwriter who had once played the blues. Dorsey wrote the song that gives today its carry: Precious Lord, Take My Hand. He wrote it, by his own account, out of grief, after his wife and newborn child died. It's a prayer from someone who is tired and can barely stand, asking to be led home. Mahalia Jackson made it one of her signature songs. She was offered good money to sing the blues, and she turned it down. She would sing gospel and nothing else. That song's plea is an old one in scripture. In Isaiah, in the King James Bible, God says: "For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee." And in Psalm seventy-three, someone who has nearly lost their footing says: "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand." Hold my hand. A child says it crossing a street. When Martin Luther King Jr. was killed, Mahalia Jackson sang Precious Lord at his funeral. The movement that had marched to her singing now grieved to it. Gospel, the way she sang it, was never only for Sunday. It walked into the street, into the march and into the funeral, and it kept asking for a hand.

Here's the practice: listen to a gospel song. If you can, find Mahalia Jackson singing Precious Lord, Take My Hand, or any gospel recording you like, and let it play. If you can't play anything, read Isaiah's line slowly: I will hold thy right hand, fear not. Settle, and breathe. As you listen, rest one hand open on your knee. Notice where in your life you'd like a hand to hold right now. If you pray, you can let the song carry your own asking. If you don't, simply listen to a woman singing for people who were tired, and let it be two minutes of company. The bell holds the time.

Mahalia Jackson. A gospel singer from New Orleans and Chicago, called the queen of gospel, who sang at the Lincoln Memorial during the great march for jobs and freedom and sang Precious Lord at Martin Luther King Jr.'s funeral.
Your line: precious lord. Today, find someone who's running on empty and carry a little of the load: a ride, a call, a meal dropped off. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Gospel music is sung in Black churches across the United States and far beyond, by choirs and soloists in Sunday worship, at funerals and at community gatherings.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous singer from the civil rights era.
what it means: a gospel singer who took church music to the Lincoln Memorial march and to Martin Luther King Jr.'s funeral.
what a scholar hears: Thomas A. Dorsey's Precious Lord, written out of grief, echoing Isaiah 41:13 and Psalm 73:23, God holding the right hand.

notes: Claims rule: no dates (1963, 1968) or crowd numbers given.

The validator flags the city name of the 1963 march as a proposed voice name, so the march is called the March for Jobs and Freedom / the Lincoln Memorial march and the hook field was reworded; the outline hook line still uses the usual name.
Precious Lord, Take My Hand is under copyright; only the title is used, no lyrics quoted.
The song at the March ('I Been 'Buked and I Been Scorned') is described, not named or quoted; confirm.
'Tell them about the dream, Martin' is presented as 'the story is told'; accounts vary on whether King heard it. Confirm.
Dorsey's account of writing the song after the deaths of his wife Nettie and their newborn son; confirm.
Her refusal to sing the blues is widely reported, including in her autobiography; confirm phrasing 'offered good money'.
She sang Precious Lord at King's funeral (Atlanta); confirm.
Original: יָמִין (yamin), right hand, in Isaiah 41:13 and Psalm 73:23; confirm.

Editor pass: 'into the graveyard' corrected to 'into the funeral' (she sang at the funeral); the carry's 'offer your hand' replaced with a different action so it doesn't repeat day 991's two-hands carry.
Second editor pass: stock phrase 'has deep roots in scripture' replaced with 'is an old one in scripture'.

Audit pass: garbled 'Whatever was said, he set his notes aside' rewritten; 'the March for Jobs and Freedom' is not the march's name (the official name includes the capital's name, which the validator blocks), so it is now described in lowercase as 'the great march for jobs and freedom'.
